content: Frameworks and regulations governing artificial intelligence (AI) are also subject to existing legal and ethical standards, including human rights obligations, bioethics laws, data protection laws, and regulatory standards. These frameworks are summarized in the report and further elaborated in other sections. Section 5 of the report outlines guiding principles established by the WHO Expert Group, which form the foundation for the analysis and findings presented. Efforts to enumerate and enforce human rights through explicit legal mechanisms are reflected in international and regional human rights conventions. These include the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights (which includes General Comment No. 14 defining the right to health), the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and regional conventions such as the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, the American Convention on Human Rights, and the European Convention on Human Rights. However, not all governments have ratified these key human rights instruments, and some have expressed reservations about specific provisions. Despite this, the human rights outlined in these international instruments establish a baseline for protecting and promoting human dignity globally. These rights are often enforced through national legislation, such as constitutions or human rights laws. Machine learning systems have the potential to advance human rights but also pose risks to core human rights standards. The Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights has issued opinions on the relationship between AI and human rights. In March 2020, the Office highlighted that AI and big data could enhance the human right to health when new technologies are designed in an accountable manner. Such technologies could provide efficient, individualized care for vulnerable populations, including assistive devices, environmental applications, and robotics. However, the Office also warned that these technologies could dehumanize care, undermine the autonomy and independence of older individuals, and pose significant risks to patient privacy, all of which conflict with the right to health. In February 2021, during a speech to the Human Rights Council, the United Nations Secretary-General expressed concerns about the growing collection and use of data during the COVID-19 pandemic. He urged governments to place human rights at the center of regulatory frameworks and legislation governing the development and use of digital technologies. Human rights organizations have interpreted and adapted existing human rights laws and standards to address the challenges and opportunities posed by AI. The Toronto Declaration addresses the impact of AI on human rights, situating AI within the universally binding framework of human rights laws and standards. It provides mechanisms for public and private sector accountability, protects individuals from discrimination, and promotes equity, diversity, and inclusion while safeguarding equality and ensuring effective remedies. In 2018, the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers issued draft recommendations to Member States on the impact of algorithmic systems on human rights. The Council is also exploring the feasibility and potential elements of a legal framework for the development, design, and application of digital technologies in accordance with its standards on human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. Legal frameworks for human rights, bioethics, and privacy adopted by various countries are applicable to several aspects of AI in health. These include Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to respect for private and family life, home, and correspondence; the Oviedo Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine, which addresses ethical principles of individual human rights and responsibilities; and the Convention for the Protection of Individuals with Regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data, along with guidelines on protecting individuals in the context of big data. Despite robust human rights standards, organizations and institutions recognize the need for better definitions of how these standards and safeguards apply to AI. New laws and jurisprudence are required to address the interaction between AI and human rights. The Council of Europe has prepared new legal guidance and, in 2019–2020, established the Ad-hoc Committee on Artificial Intelligence to conduct broad multi-stakeholder consultations. This initiative aims to determine the feasibility and potential elements of a legal framework for AI design and application in line with the Council’s standards on human rights, democracy, and the rule of law. Additionally, in 2019, the Council of Europe released Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence and Data Protection, emphasizing the protection of human dignity and safeguarding human rights and fundamental freedoms. Data protection laws are rights-based approaches that establish standards for regulating data processing to protect individual rights and impose obligations on data controllers and processors. These laws increasingly recognize the right of individuals not to be subjected to decisions made solely by automated processes. Over 100 countries have enacted data protection laws, with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) being a prominent example. In the United States, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) addresses privacy and security in health data. Some standards and guidelines are specifically designed to manage the use of personal data in AI, such as the Ibero-American Data Protection Network’s General Recommendations for the Processing of Personal Data in Artificial Intelligence and specific guidelines for compliance with data protection principles in AI projects. Laws and policies governing health data collection, processing, analysis, transfer, and use include recommendations from the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers on protecting health-related data and the African Union’s convention on cybersecurity and personal data protection. These frameworks emphasize the need for adequate regulation to ensure trust in digitalization. In February 2021, the African Academy of Sciences and the African Union Development Agency released recommendations for data and biospecimen governance in Africa, promoting a participant-centered approach to research involving human participants while enabling ethical research practices. Regulations governing the transfer of data across countries include provisions in trade agreements, intellectual property rules for data ownership, and competition laws addressing data accumulation and control. General principles for AI development and use have been proposed by various intergovernmental organizations and countries. These principles emphasize transparency, justice, fairness, non-maleficence, and responsibility, while other principles such as privacy, solidarity, human dignity, and sustainability are less frequently represented. The WHO has not yet proposed specific ethical principles for AI use in health. However, the Astana Declaration, issued during the WHO Global Conference on Primary Health Care, includes principles for using digital technology to improve access to healthcare, enhance service delivery, and ensure patient safety. UNESCO has also provided guidance on the ethical implications of AI and big data in health, supported by expert committees such as the World Commission on the Ethics of Scientific Knowledge and Technology and the International Bioethics Committee. Other initiatives include the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) Code of Conduct for data-driven health technologies and the African Union’s High-level Panel on Emerging Technologies, which is preparing guidance on AI use to promote economic development and healthcare. Bioethics laws and policies play a critical role in regulating AI use. Recent revisions to bioethics laws, such as France’s 2019 update, address the rapid growth of digital technologies in healthcare. These laws establish standards for human oversight and require evaluation by patients and clinicians at critical points in AI development and deployment. Regulatory considerations for AI technologies are being developed by health regulatory authorities to ensure safety, efficacy, and appropriate use in healthcare and therapeutic development. The WHO expert group has identified key areas for stakeholders to consider, including documentation, transparency, risk management, data quality, validation, engagement, collaboration, and privacy.
